title: d- and f-Block Elements
tagline: Electronic configuration, trends, compounds and applications of the transition and inner transition elements in the ISC XII syllabus.

overview.intro: The d-block elements, often called transition elements, occupy the middle of the periodic table and are defined by a partly filled d subshell in the atom or in at least one common ion. The first transition series, from scandium to zinc, shows the characteristic properties that arise from this electronic structure: variable oxidation states, formation of coloured ions, paramagnetism, catalytic activity, alloy formation and the tendency to form complexes. These properties are all consequences of the comparable energies of the (n-1)d and ns electrons and of the availability of d orbitals for bonding. This chapter surveys the general trends across the 3d series, the formation of interstitial compounds, and the preparation, properties and uses of two important compounds, potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate. It then turns to the f-block, the inner transition elements, which include the lanthanoids and actinoids. The lanthanoids are notable for the steady decrease in ionic radius known as the lanthanoid contraction, which has consequences for the chemistry of the elements that follow them, while the actinoids are characterised by a wider range of oxidation states and by radioactivity.

learn.title: Electronic configuration and general trends in the 3d series

blocks.text: The elements of the first transition series have the general valence configuration (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2, with chromium and copper adopting the half-filled and completely filled d configurations 3d5 4s1 and 3d10 4s1 because of the extra stability of those arrangements. A transition element is one that has an incompletely filled d subshell in its atom or in at least one of its common ions; by this definition zinc, with a filled 3d10 configuration in both the atom and the Zn2+ ion, is often not counted as a typical transition element, although it is placed in the d-block. The (n-1)d and ns electrons are close in energy, so more than one electron can be lost in chemical reactions, which is the origin of variable oxidation states.

Across the 3d series the atomic and ionic radii decrease only gradually from left to right, because the increasing nuclear charge is partly screened by the added d electrons, and near the end of the series the radii may even increase slightly because of electron-electron repulsion in the paired d orbitals. The ionisation enthalpies rise irregularly for the same reason. The metallic character is high, with good electrical and thermal conductivity and metallic lustre, because the outer electrons are delocalised in a metallic lattice. Densities are generally high and melting and boiling points are high, reflecting strong metallic bonding involving both s and d electrons, with a dip near the middle of the series where half-filled d subshells give a particularly stable arrangement of the metal atoms.

items: Variable oxidation states arise because (n-1)d and ns electrons have comparable energies and can both be involved in bonding.
The most common oxidation state in the 3d series is +2, formed by loss of the two 4s electrons.
Higher oxidation states are stabilised in compounds with highly electronegative elements such as oxygen and fluorine.
Manganese shows the widest range, from +2 to +7, reflecting the availability of all five 3d and both 4s electrons.
Scandium shows only +3 and zinc shows only +2, consistent with their limited d electron involvement.
The stability of a particular oxidation state depends on the element, the ligands or anions present and the medium.

learn.title: Colour, magnetic properties, catalysis and interstitial compounds

blocks.text: Most transition metal ions are coloured in aqueous solution and in their compounds, whereas ions with empty or completely filled d subshells, such as Sc3+, Ti4+, Cu+ and Zn2+, are colourless. The colour arises from d-d transitions: in the presence of surrounding ligands or anions the d orbitals split into sets of different energy, and an electron can absorb visible light and be promoted from a lower to a higher d orbital. The colour observed is the complementary colour of the light absorbed. The exact colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the nature of the ligands, which is why the same metal can give differently coloured compounds in different environments.

Paramagnetism in transition elements is caused by unpaired d electrons, each of which behaves like a tiny magnet. The magnetic moment is given approximately by the spin-only formula mu = sqrt(n(n + 2)) Bohr magneton, where n is the number of unpaired electrons, so measuring the magnetic moment gives information about the number of unpaired electrons. Ions with no unpaired electrons are diamagnetic and are weakly repelled by a magnetic field. Many transition metals and their compounds act as catalysts, for example iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process and nickel in hydrogenation, because they can adopt variable oxidation states and can form intermediate compounds with the reactants, providing a pathway of lower activation energy. Interstitial compounds form when small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon or nitrogen occupy the spaces in a metal lattice; they are typically hard, have high melting points, retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert, and steel is an important example.

items: Colour requires an incompletely filled d subshell so that d-d transitions are possible.
Colourless ions include Sc3+ (d0), Ti4+ (d0), Zn2+ (d10) and Cu+ (d10).
Paramagnetic substances are attracted into a magnetic field; diamagnetic substances are weakly repelled.
Spin-only magnetic moment mu = sqrt(n(n + 2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
Catalytic activity is linked to variable oxidation states and to the ability to form complexes and adsorb reactants on the surface.
Interstitial compounds are non-stoichiometric, very hard, chemically inert and retain metallic conductivity.

items.text: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Fe2+ in its high-spin state.
items.note: Fe2+ has the configuration 3d6 with four unpaired electrons in the high-spin state, so mu = sqrt(4 x 6) = sqrt(24) = 4.90 BM. This matches the observed paramagnetism of many iron(II) compounds.

items.text: Explain why Cu+ salts are usually colourless while Cu2+ salts are coloured.
items.note: Cu+ has a 3d10 configuration with no vacant d orbital of suitable energy, so no d-d transition is possible and the ion is colourless. Cu2+ has a 3d9 configuration with one vacancy, so a d-d transition can absorb visible light and the compounds appear blue or green.

blocks.text: Potassium dichromate, K2Cr2O7, is an orange crystalline solid in which chromium is in the +6 oxidation state. It is prepared from chromite ore by fusion with sodium carbonate in air to give sodium chromate, acidification to sodium dichromate, and treatment with potassium chloride to precipitate the less soluble potassium salt. In aqueous solution dichromate and chromate ions are in equilibrium, Cr2O7^2- + H2O gives 2 CrO4^2- + 2 H+, with the orange dichromate favoured in acidic solution and the yellow chromate favoured in alkaline solution. Potassium dichromate is a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium, being reduced from chromium(VI) to chromium(III): Cr2O7^2- + 14 H+ + 6 e- gives 2 Cr3+ + 7 H2O. It oxidises iodide to iodine, iron(II) to iron(III), sulphite to sulphate and hydrogen sulphide to sulphur, and it is used in volumetric analysis, in leather tanning and in the preparation of chrome alum.

Potassium permanganate, KMnO4, is a deep purple crystalline solid in which manganese is in the +7 oxidation state. It is prepared from pyrolusite, MnO2, by fusion with potassium hydroxide in the presence of an oxidising agent to give green potassium manganate, which is then oxidised electrolytically or by chlorine or ozone to permanganate. It is a very strong oxidising agent in all media, but the product depends on the pH. In acidic solution it is reduced to Mn2+, MnO4^- + 8 H+ + 5 e- gives Mn2+ + 4 H2O, and the purple colour is discharged; in neutral or faintly alkaline solution it is reduced to MnO2, a brown precipitate; in strongly alkaline solution it is reduced to the green manganate ion. It oxidises oxalate, iron(II), iodide and sulphite, and it is used as a disinfectant, in volumetric analysis and in organic chemistry for the oxidation of alkenes and side chains.

items: Dichromate-chromate equilibrium: orange Cr2O7^2- in acid, yellow CrO4^2- in alkali.
In acidic solution, one mole of dichromate accepts six electrons and oxidises six moles of Fe2+ or three moles of iodide ions to iodine.
Permanganate in acidic medium: MnO4^- + 8 H+ + 5 e- gives Mn2+ + 4 H2O.
Permanganate in neutral or faintly alkaline medium: MnO4^- + 2 H2O + 3 e- gives MnO2 + 4 OH^-.
Permanganate in strongly alkaline medium: MnO4^- + e- gives MnO4^2-.
Both compounds are powerful oxidising agents, but permanganate is the stronger and acts in a wider range of conditions.

items.text: Write the ionic equation for the oxidation of iron(II) by acidified potassium dichromate.
items.note: Cr2O7^2- + 14 H+ + 6 Fe2+ gives 2 Cr3+ + 7 H2O + 6 Fe3+. The orange solution turns green as chromium(III) is formed, and each dichromate ion oxidises six iron(II) ions.

items.text: How many moles of oxalic acid are oxidised by one mole of acidified potassium permanganate?
items.note: The half-reactions are MnO4^- + 8 H+ + 5 e- gives Mn2+ + 4 H2O and C2O4^2- gives 2 CO2 + 2 e-. Balancing electrons gives 2 MnO4^- reacting with 5 C2O4^2-, so one mole of permanganate oxidises 2.5 moles of oxalic acid.

blocks.text: The lanthanoids are the fourteen elements from cerium to lutetium in which electrons are progressively added to the 4f subshell. They are typically placed as a separate row below the main periodic table, together with lanthanum which often precedes them and resembles them chemically. The general valence configuration is 4f1-14 5d0-1 6s2, and the most common oxidation state is +3, formed by loss of the two 6s electrons and one 4f or 5d electron. Some elements also show +2 or +4 states when doing so gives an empty, half-filled or completely filled 4f subshell, for example cerium in +4 and europium in +2. The lanthanoids are silvery-white metals, reactive, and their compounds are often coloured and paramagnetic because of unpaired 4f electrons.

The lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii from lanthanum to lutetium. As the nuclear charge increases across the series, electrons are added to the 4f orbitals, but 4f electrons shield the outer electrons poorly because of the diffuse shape of the f orbitals. The result is that the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer electrons increases steadily, pulling them closer and reducing the size. This contraction has important consequences: the elements that follow the lanthanoids in the periodic table, such as hafnium and tantalum, have almost the same atomic radii as the elements directly above them, zirconium and niobium, which makes them very similar chemically and difficult to separate. The basicity of the lanthanoid hydroxides also decreases slightly from lanthanum to lutetium as the ionic size decreases.

items: Lanthanoids fill the 4f subshell and most commonly exhibit the +3 oxidation state.
Lanthanoid contraction is caused by poor shielding of the increasing nuclear charge by 4f electrons.
Consequences include the similarity in size and chemistry of second and third row transition elements such as Zr and Hf.
The contraction also makes the separation of individual lanthanoids difficult because their properties vary only gradually.
Lanthanoid compounds are often coloured and paramagnetic due to unpaired 4f electrons.
Mischmetal, an alloy of lanthanoids, is used in lighter flints and in some steels.

items.text: Why do zirconium and hafnium have almost identical atomic radii and very similar chemical properties?
items.note: Hafnium follows the lanthanoids in the periodic table, so its expected increase in size relative to zirconium is cancelled by the lanthanoid contraction. The resulting similarity in size and in charge density makes the two elements hard to separate and very alike in their chemistry.

blocks.text: The actinoids are the fourteen elements from thorium to lawrencium in which the 5f subshell is progressively filled. They resemble the lanthanoids in having partly filled f orbitals and in showing a contraction in ionic radii across the series, but there are important differences. All actinoids are radioactive, and many of the elements beyond uranium are synthetic, produced in nuclear reactors or accelerators. The 5f electrons are less effectively shielded than 4f electrons and are more available for bonding, so the actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states, from +3 up to +6 or +7 in the early members such as uranium and neptunium, whereas the lanthanoids are dominated by +3. The early actinoids also form complexes and show greater variability in their chemistry than the lanthanoids do.

blocks.caption: Table: Comparison of lanthanoids and actinoids
rows: 4f electrons more buried and less involved in bonding

items.text: Why do actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids?
items.note: In actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s electrons have comparable energies and the 5f electrons are less effectively shielded from the nucleus, so more of them can participate in bonding. In lanthanoids the 4f electrons are more deeply buried, which restricts the chemistry largely to the +3 state.

keyPoints: Transition elements have partly filled d subshells in the atom or in a common ion and show variable oxidation states.
Across the 3d series, atomic and ionic radii decrease gradually and metallic character remains high.
Colour in transition metal ions arises from d-d transitions in an incompletely filled d subshell.
Paramagnetism is due to unpaired electrons, with spin-only magnetic moment sqrt(n(n + 2)) Bohr magneton.
Transition metals and their compounds act as catalysts because of variable oxidation states and complex formation.
Interstitial compounds are hard, high-melting and chemically inert materials formed by small atoms in metal lattices.
Potassium dichromate is an orange oxidising agent in acidic medium, reduced from Cr(VI) to Cr(III).
Potassium permanganate is a purple oxidising agent whose reduction product depends on the pH of the medium.
Lanthanoids predominantly show the +3 oxidation state and exhibit the lanthanoid contraction due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.
The lanthanoid contraction explains the close similarity in size and chemistry of Zr and Hf.
Actinoids are all radioactive and show a wider range of oxidation states than lanthanoids because 5f electrons are more available for bonding.
examFocus: Explaining variable oxidation states, colour, paramagnetism and catalytic activity in terms of d electron configuration.
Calculating the spin-only magnetic moment from the number of unpaired electrons.
Writing balanced ionic equations for the oxidising actions of K2Cr2O7 and KMnO4 in different media.
Describing the dichromate-chromate equilibrium and the effect of pH.
Explaining the lanthanoid contraction and its consequences, especially the similarity of Zr and Hf.
Comparing lanthanoids and actinoids in oxidation states, radioactivity and complex formation.
Identifying colourless and coloured transition metal ions from their electronic configurations.

vocabulary.meaning: An element that has an incompletely filled d subshell in its atom or in at least one of its common oxidation states.
The block of elements in the periodic table in which the differentiating electron enters a d orbital.
The ability of an element, especially a transition metal, to exist in more than one oxidation state in its compounds.
The promotion of an electron from a lower-energy d orbital to a higher-energy d orbital by absorption of light, producing colour.
The property of being attracted into a magnetic field due to the presence of unpaired electrons.
The property of being weakly repelled by a magnetic field when all electrons are paired.
The magnetic moment calculated from unpaired electrons alone as sqrt(n(n + 2)) Bohr magneton.
A hard, non-stoichiometric compound formed when small atoms such as H, C or N occupy holes in a metal lattice.
The fourteen elements from cerium to lutetium in which the 4f subshell is progressively filled.
The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series due to poor shielding by 4f electrons.
The fourteen elements from thorium to lawrencium in which the 5f subshell is progressively filled, all radioactive.
A substance that accepts electrons and is reduced, causing another substance to be oxidised.

The radius decreases gradually at first, remains nearly constant through the middle of the series, and increases slightly towards the end. Adding acid shifts the equilibrium towards dichromate, while adding alkali shifts it towards chromate, illustrating the effect of pH on the species present.

chromium in +6 oxidation state in both ions

questions.prompt: Which of the following elements is not generally regarded as a typical transition element?
questions.answer: Zinc
questions.explanation: A transition element has an incompletely filled d subshell in its atom or in at least one common ion. Zinc has the configuration 3d10 in both the atom and the Zn2+ ion, so it does not meet this definition even though it lies in the d-block.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming every d-block element is a transition element.

questions.prompt: The colour of transition metal ions is mainly due to:
options: the high density of the metal
the metallic bonding in the lattice
questions.answer: d-d electronic transitions
questions.explanation: In an incompletely filled d subshell, electrons can absorb visible light and move between split d orbitals. The complementary colour of the absorbed light is observed, which is why ions such as Cu2+ and Fe3+ are coloured.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the colour to the emission of light rather than to absorption.

questions.prompt: The spin-only magnetic moment of an ion with four unpaired electrons is closest to:
questions.explanation: Using mu = sqrt(n(n + 2)) with n = 4 gives sqrt(24) = 4.90 Bohr magneton. Three unpaired electrons give 3.87 BM and five give 5.92 BM.
questions.commonMistake: Using n instead of n(n + 2) inside the square root.

questions.prompt: In acidic solution, the dichromate ion acts as an oxidising agent and is reduced to:
questions.answer: Cr3+
questions.explanation: In acidic medium the half-reaction is Cr2O7^2- + 14 H+ + 6 e- gives 2 Cr3+ + 7 H2O, so chromium is reduced from +6 to +3 and the solution turns green.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing chromate, which is formed in alkaline rather than acidic solution.

questions.prompt: The lanthanoid contraction is mainly due to:
options: poor shielding of the nuclear charge by 4f electrons
perfect shielding of the nuclear charge by 4f electrons
a decrease in the number of protons across the series
the large size of the 4f orbitals
questions.answer: poor shielding of the nuclear charge by 4f electrons
questions.explanation: As the atomic number increases across the lanthanoids, the added 4f electrons do not effectively shield the increasing nuclear charge, so the outer electrons are pulled in more strongly and the atomic and ionic radii decrease steadily.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that adding electrons must increase the atomic size.

questions.prompt: When potassium permanganate acts as an oxidising agent in strongly alkaline medium, the manganese-containing product is:
questions.answer: manganate ion, MnO4^2-
questions.explanation: In strongly alkaline solution permanganate is reduced by one electron to the green manganate ion MnO4^2-. In acidic solution it gives Mn2+, and in neutral or faintly alkaline solution it gives brown MnO2.
questions.commonMistake: Giving Mn2+, which is the product in acidic solution.

questions.prompt: Zirconium and hafnium have very similar atomic radii because of:
options: their position in the same period
questions.answer: the lanthanoid contraction
questions.explanation: Hafnium follows the lanthanoids, so the expected increase in size is offset by the steady decrease in radius across the 4f series. As a result Zr and Hf are almost the same size and show very similar chemistry.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing the similarity to their being in the same group without mentioning the contraction.

questions.prompt: Compared with lanthanoids, actinoids generally show:
options: a wider range of oxidation states
a stronger tendency to show only the +3 state
questions.answer: a wider range of oxidation states
questions.explanation: In actinoids the 5f, 6d and 7s electrons are closer in energy and the 5f electrons are more available for bonding, so oxidation states such as +4, +5 and +6 are common in addition to +3. All actinoids are radioactive.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming actinoids behave exactly like lanthanoids because both are f-block elements.

questions.prompt: The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series is known as the ______ contraction.
questions.answer: lanthanoid
questions.explanation: The lanthanoid contraction results from the poor shielding of the increasing nuclear charge by 4f electrons, causing a gradual decrease in size from lanthanum to lutetium.
questions.commonMistake: Writing actinoid contraction, which is a different though related phenomenon.

questions.prompt: In acidic solution, potassium dichromate oxidises iron(II) ions to ______ ions.
questions.answer: iron(III)
questions.explanation: Dichromate is a strong oxidising agent in acidic medium and removes one electron from each Fe2+ ion, converting it to Fe3+ while chromium is reduced from +6 to +3.
questions.commonMistake: Writing iron metal instead of iron(III).

questions.prompt: Compounds formed when small atoms such as hydrogen, carbon or nitrogen occupy holes in a metal lattice are called ______ compounds.
questions.answer: interstitial
questions.explanation: Interstitial compounds are typically hard, have high melting points, retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert because the small atoms fit into the spaces of the metal lattice without greatly disturbing it.
questions.commonMistake: Writing intermetallic compounds, which are alloys of two or more metals.

questions.prompt: Why do transition elements show variable oxidation states?
questions.answer: In transition elements the energies of the (n-1)d and ns electrons are comparable, so different numbers of these electrons can participate in bonding under different conditions. This allows the same element to form stable compounds in more than one oxidation state, for example iron as +2 and +3 and manganese from +2 to +7.
questions.explanation: The small energy difference between the inner d and outer s electrons means that losing only the s electrons or losing both s and some d electrons can both be energetically feasible.
questions.commonMistake: Attributing variable oxidation states only to the loss of s electrons.

questions.prompt: Explain why Zn2+ salts are colourless whereas Cu2+ salts are coloured.
questions.answer: Zn2+ has the electronic configuration 3d10 with a completely filled d subshell, so no d-d transition is possible and it does not absorb visible light. Cu2+ has the configuration 3d9 with one vacancy in the d subshell, so an electron can be promoted between split d orbitals by absorbing visible light and the compounds appear coloured.
questions.explanation: Colour in transition metal ions requires both an incompletely filled d subshell and an energy gap between d orbitals that corresponds to visible light, a condition met by Cu2+ but not by Zn2+.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that all transition metal ions are coloured without considering the d electron count.

questions.prompt: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Mn2+ in its high-spin state.
questions.answer: Mn2+ has the configuration 3d5 with five unpaired electrons in the high-spin state. The spin-only magnetic moment is mu = sqrt(n(n + 2)) = sqrt(5 x 7) = sqrt(35) = 5.92 BM.
questions.explanation: Each unpaired electron contributes to the magnetic moment, and with five unpaired d electrons Mn2+ has the maximum spin-only moment among the 3d ions.
questions.commonMistake: Using the atomic number or the total number of d electrons instead of the number of unpaired electrons.

questions.prompt: State the effect of adding acid and of adding alkali to an aqueous solution of potassium dichromate.
questions.answer: Adding acid to the orange dichromate solution keeps or intensifies the orange colour because the equilibrium Cr2O7^2- + H2O gives 2 CrO4^2- + 2 H+ shifts to the left, favouring dichromate. Adding alkali removes hydrogen ions and shifts the equilibrium to the right, converting the orange dichromate into the yellow chromate ion CrO4^2-.
questions.explanation: The two ions contain chromium in the same +6 oxidation state and are interconverted by a change in pH rather than by a redox reaction.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the colour change as a reduction or oxidation of chromium.

questions.prompt: Explain the catalytic properties of transition metals with suitable examples.
questions.answer: Transition metals and their compounds are effective catalysts because they can adopt variable oxidation states and can form unstable intermediate compounds with reactants, providing an alternative pathway of lower activation energy. Their ability to adsorb reactant molecules on the surface and to use vacant d orbitals for bonding also promotes reaction. Examples include finely divided iron in the Haber process for ammonia synthesis, vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process for sulphuric acid manufacture, and finely divided nickel in the hydrogenation of vegetable oils. In each case the catalyst participates in the reaction sequence but is regenerated at the end.
questions.explanation: The combination of variable oxidation states and surface adsorption allows transition metals to bring reactants together and to weaken bonds, which lowers the activation energy without altering the overall thermodynamics.
questions.commonMistake: Stating that catalysts work only by adsorption and ignoring the role of variable oxidation states.

questions.prompt: Describe the preparation of potassium permanganate from pyrolusite ore and write the relevant equations.
questions.answer: Pyrolusite, MnO2, is fused with potassium hydroxide in the presence of air or an oxidising agent such as potassium nitrate to form green potassium manganate: 2 MnO2 + 4 KOH + O2 gives 2 K2MnO4 + 2 H2O. The manganate is then oxidised to permanganate either electrolytically or by passing chlorine or ozone through its solution: 2 K2MnO4 + Cl2 gives 2 KMnO4 + 2 KCl. On concentration and cooling, dark purple crystals of potassium permanganate separate. The overall process converts manganese from +4 in the ore to +6 in manganate and finally to +7 in permanganate.
questions.explanation: The preparation is carried out in two stages because direct oxidation of MnO2 to permanganate is difficult, while oxidation of manganate to permanganate is straightforward in alkaline solution.
questions.commonMistake: Writing the final product as manganese dioxide instead of permanganate.

questions.prompt: What is the lanthanoid contraction? Explain its cause and give two consequences.
questions.answer: The lanthanoid contraction is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the elements from lanthanum to lutetium. It is caused by the poor shielding of the increasing nuclear charge by the 4f electrons, so the effective nuclear charge experienced by the outer electrons rises across the series and pulls them closer to the nucleus. One consequence is that zirconium and hafnium, which lie in the same group but in different periods, have almost identical atomic radii and very similar chemical properties, making them difficult to separate. Another consequence is the gradual decrease in basicity of the lanthanoid hydroxides from La(OH)3 to Lu(OH)3 as the ionic size decreases and the covalent character increases.
questions.explanation: Because f orbitals are diffuse, the added electrons do not compensate for the added protons, so the contraction is cumulative across all fourteen elements and has effects well beyond the lanthanoid series itself.
questions.commonMistake: Stating the contraction without explaining the role of poor shielding by 4f electrons.

questions.prompt: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of Cr3+ and state whether it is paramagnetic or diamagnetic.
questions.answer: Chromium has atomic number 24 with configuration [Ar] 3d5 4s1. Cr3+ is formed by losing two 4s electrons and one 3d electron, giving [Ar] 3d3 with three unpaired electrons. The spin-only magnetic moment is mu = sqrt(n(n + 2)) = sqrt(3 x 5) = sqrt(15) = 3.87 BM. Because it has unpaired electrons, Cr3+ is paramagnetic.
questions.explanation: The number of unpaired electrons determines both the magnitude of the magnetic moment and whether the ion is attracted into a magnetic field. Three unpaired electrons in the 3d subshell give the characteristic moment of chromium(III) compounds.
questions.commonMistake: Counting all d electrons instead of only the unpaired ones.

questions.prompt: Write the balanced ionic equation for the oxidation of iodide ions by acidified potassium dichromate and identify the change in oxidation state of chromium.
questions.answer: The half-reactions are Cr2O7^2- + 14 H+ + 6 e- gives 2 Cr3+ + 7 H2O and 2 I- gives I2 + 2 e-. Multiplying the iodide half-reaction by three and adding gives Cr2O7^2- + 14 H+ + 6 I- gives 2 Cr3+ + 7 H2O + 3 I2. Chromium is reduced from +6 in dichromate to +3 in Cr3+, a decrease of three units per chromium atom.
questions.explanation: Six electrons are transferred in total, matching the six iodide ions oxidised to three molecules of iodine. The solution changes from orange to green as chromium(III) forms.
questions.commonMistake: Failing to balance the electrons and writing only one molecule of iodine.

questions.prompt: A solution of KMnO4 is used to titrate 20.0 mL of 0.10 M oxalic acid solution in acidic medium. Calculate the volume of 0.02 M KMnO4 required.
questions.answer: In acidic medium, 2 MnO4^- react with 5 C2O4^2-, so the mole ratio is 2:5. Moles of oxalic acid = 0.10 x 20.0 / 1000 = 0.00200 mol. Moles of KMnO4 required = (2/5) x 0.00200 = 0.000800 mol. Volume of 0.02 M KMnO4 = 0.000800 / 0.02 = 0.0400 L = 40.0 mL.
questions.explanation: The stoichiometry follows from balancing the electrons in the two half-reactions: permanganate gains five electrons per ion and oxalate loses two, so two permanganate ions oxidise five oxalate ions.
questions.commonMistake: Using a 1:1 mole ratio instead of the 2:5 ratio from the balanced redox equation.

questions.prompt: Explain why actinoids show a greater range of oxidation states than lanthanoids, and state two other differences between the two series.
questions.answer: Actinoids show a wider range of oxidation states because their 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals have comparable energies and the 5f electrons are less deeply buried and more available for bonding than the 4f electrons of lanthanoids. As a result, oxidation states from +3 up to +6 or +7 occur in early actinoids such as uranium, whereas lanthanoids are dominated by +3. Two other differences are that all actinoids are radioactive while most lanthanoids are not, and actinoids have a greater tendency to form complexes because their 5f orbitals can participate more readily in bonding.
questions.explanation: The key distinction is the relative accessibility of the f electrons: 4f electrons in lanthanoids are shielded by outer electrons and behave more like core electrons, while 5f electrons in actinoids are closer in energy to the valence shell and take part in bonding.
questions.commonMistake: Listing differences without giving the underlying reason in terms of 4f and 5f electron availability.
